utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question relates to the conflict. During the conflict were there companies that kept producing and exporting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Produce, no, or very little, but they exported the stocks of merchandise that they had. So the salt had been produced before the war, and it was put into warehouses. A half of those companies were not really operational due to most of the employees being drafted. So they only were able to dispose of their stock. So the steel plant of Zenica had a huge stock of construction iron, and this salt mine had a stock of salt. And after the conflict broke out, they sold those goods to Croatia, Slovenia. Mostly it was to these two countries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me take the example of Zenica. You said that there was a company in Zenica that manufactured iron. There is indeed a well-known steel plant in Zenica. During the conflict, if I understood you properly, there was export to Croatia. If that was so, since the border was being controlled by the HVO, how did these companies transit their goods through Herzegovina? Would they ask for approval from the HVO? Did they have to pay export taxes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Bosnia-Herzegovina there were no export taxes. There were none in HZ HB either. If a company had sold goods to a firm in Split, Croatia, the truck would come to the customs office in Mostar or any other customs office in HZ HB that were operational, let's say Tomislavgrad, and there, based on the invoice they had and other documents, the export customs declaration would be made. They -- the exporter had to find a forwarding agent to make that declaration for the exportation of goods, and that documentation had to be stamped by the customs administration of the HZ HB. Then they could go on to Croatia and would continue the process of clearing customs in Croatia under Croatian regulations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And maybe I wasn't quite complete in my earlier questioning. You said that there was communications between Herzegovina and Zenica. Was there a linkage between the SDK of the two? In other words, if you understand my question, from Mostar was there -- was there a direct link to Zenica at the time?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no -- not even a link between Mostar and the municipalities and areas belonging to the HZ HB in Central Bosnia. So there was no communication with Central Bosnia at all. This applies to Zenica also. So there was no -- no way of effecting payment from Mostar to Zenica or from Mostar to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But when you indicated earlier, because this is -- and it may be something that's being lost in translation because as I understand, "communication" in your language, you know, has various meanings. Earlier you indicated there was communication between Herzegovina and Zenica. What exactly did you mean by that? Are we talking about road communication, telecommunication, radio communication? So please explain to us what did you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I speak about the payment system, I always mean telecommunications. That is telecommunication lines used by the SDK to effect payment. A road is a communication too. It was possible to go to Zenica physically. A truck could drive to Zenica. But payment could exclusively be made either in cash or through non-resident accounts, but direct payment between the SDK and Mostar and Zenica was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I think I cleared that point up. I'm clear. I don't know if anybody else is un-clear. And then finally I think the last part of this document we see 20 per cent looks like it's going to be paid in some sort of a bartering system, exchange of commodities. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, this contract was based on a template, and companies were partly paid in kind in order to be able to distribute, say, flour, sugar, and other commodities to their employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at 1D 00140. 1D 00140. This is December 1992. This is a decree on payment transactions via accounts and subaccounts with the SDK. If we could look at this. And a brief explanation. I'm going to ask you to look at Article 1, 2, and perhaps even comment on Article 11. That may be of some assistance.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're speaking about a decree that defines how payments through giro accounts are to be made, giro accounts and subaccounts. In Croatian dinars and BH dinars and any other currencies that we used as official currencies in -- for payment. First of all, the Deutschmark. I must first point to Article 11. It is customary in the banking world but also in the SDK of the former Yugoslavia to distinguish between cash and money on accounts, I mean the amounts on accounts because money on accounts is not always -- does not always have cash coverage. That is normal in countries that have a Central Bank, primary mission, et cetera. Article 11 says, in simplified terms, the -- at the SDK HZ HB, at the end of each working day the balance of each giro account and subaccount on the one hand and the cash balance must be equal. What does that mean? That all money that goes through the SDK must have cash coverage. We only used Croatian dinars and Deutschmarks, but we didn't have any power over those currencies. One of the great problems in the former Yugoslavia was when pressurised by politics, the SDK allowed some accounts, that payment is effected from some accounts although there was no money on those accounts. This is like -- this is as if the Central Bank had issued a new quantity of money, if I can explain it that way, and that eroded the confidence in those services, et cetera. Now, we mostly used Croatian and German currencies. We could not allow anything similar to happen, and that's why we introduced this obligation to check the balances on a daily basis and report about that because we wanted to show that money flows through the SDK only for the purpose of controlling the payment of taxes, contributions and other payments that were prescribed at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would be grateful if such complex matters could be expressed and explained more slowly. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm told that while you're eloquent in your explanations, you need to be rather slower in articulating your thoughts, because these are rather complex matters that some of us who are less acquainted with this system are having a difficulty following, let alone translating. If I could just ask you to comment on Article 12, because Article 12 makes reference to a law on financial operations of the federative republic -- the Socialist Federative Republic Of Yugoslavia, and could you please tell us, because this is now 17 December 1992. Why is it making reference to this particular law, and what is this law about, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was one of the basic laws for the functioning of the payment system, for the opening of accounts for effecting payment inside the country and so on. It was a large piece of legislation. And this decree mostly regulates the segment I spoke about, and the rest -- to all the rest the provisions of this Yugoslav law had to be applied. Yugoslavia, of course, had its own currency, its Central Bank and other mechanisms to exert control over the currency. This law was also adopted or taken over by the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Unless there are any questions concerning this particular document, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this is a question that doesn't relate specifically to this document, but I'm trying to understand the intricate mechanisms that prevailed at the time. Several currencies were in circulation at the time, the Deutschmark, the BH dinar, the Croatian dinar. Now, in Mostar did you not circulate coupons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The BH dinar was called coupon for a while. It was called that because it wasn't real money. It was printed based on decision of the Ministry of Finance rather than the Central Bank. That's why colloquially it was -- it was occasionally called a coupon. What's meant was the BH dinar. We never issued coupons. In other words, we never printed money.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In statistical terms, according to you in the field, in the percentage terms as far as these various currencies are concerned, how many Deutschmark, how many Croatian dinars, BH dinars or perhaps US dollars were there circulated? Do you have -- do you have some empirical data you could give us concerning the circulation of these currencies? I assume that there was a black market. And on the black market transactions were carried out in various currencies, I assume.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me first say that in the era of HZ HB there was no black market. As is stated in Article 11, there was no need for the conversion of one currency into the other -- into another, because all currencies that were present at the time could be used for payment if so desired. So you have no need to convert dinars into Deutschmarks because you could pay in Deutschmarks. Or you could also pay in dollars. I'm mentioning these because these were the most common currencies. About the quantity of money in terms of value, I can say that the greatest quality was in Deutschmarks, then in Croatian dinars, then dollars, and then BH dinars in terms of value, I say. In terms of quantity, I cannot say anything off the top of my head now. When in 1996 we took the decision at federation level about the unification of the payment system, in other words, the linking up of the HZ HB SDK with the SDK in the areas controlled by the army of BiH, then all currencies were practically accepted and payments between these two systems were first -- at first effected in Deutschmarks, and when the system started functioning as one, the German mark was the only currency left, and later it was the convertible mark, the currency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. At the moment when these two systems were -- were turned into one, when a closing balance had to be made, and we did that together with people from the World Bank and people from the International Monetary Fund, it was established that in the area of the HZ HB and its SDK, there was no difference between money -- the money on accounts and the cash in -- in the safes, whereas in areas controlled by the army of BiH, the difference established was 24 million Deutschmarks. That is the difference between the money printed and the cash -- and the cash at hand under this difference had to be compensated to regain confidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since international officials were present, the Spanish battalion and the EU representatives, how did they pay? Did they use US dollars, DEM, Croatian dinars, or BH dinars? How -- or what currency did they use?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the most part in German marks. The sales contract for the salt was paid in cash in German marks by the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The international organisations had cash, did they? They hadn't opened an account somewhere, had they? Everything was being paid in cash. Is that how it happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We'll move on to the next document, P 01579. And we can see that is decree on border crossings and traffic. Now, this is I believe March 1993. It's actually signed in February, published in March, February 26, 1993. If you could focus first on Article 2. Please tell us what is this decree about and why was it necessary since we already have a border crossing from the previous legal instrument that we saw?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a decree that is within the purview of the department of the interior, so it is mostly regulated by the jurisdiction that is managed by the police, and it becomes necessary when the system is being built in order to define the border belt which is under the control of the border police, the police controlling the border, and this is an area where the border police can intervene. This law was adopted, the law on the crossing of the state border and movement in the border belt. The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in turn adopted the federal law, the Yugoslav law, and this pertains only to a segment of the border belt of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina that is in the area of the HZ HB. The area facing the area controlled by the BH army was not treated as a border area to which the provisions of this law would apply.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And -- and I believe that was an earlier question that was posed by Judge Trechsel concerning whether there were those sorts of borders on that site. If we look at Article 3 it says that: "The proposal of the head of the HVO HZ HB defence department or the HVO HZ HB department of interior, the Croatian Defence Council may determine that the border area shall be more than 100 metres wide." So again we see a proposal, this is a proposal, and of course the HZ HB -- the HVO HZ HB may, it's discretionary, determine that it may be wider than a hundred metres. Why was this necessary, if you recall, if you know?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, this is in order to control illegal border crossings, illegal crossing of goods, weapons, individuals, and it is usual practice to have an area that is 100 metres deep. This is a belt where the border services can respond to a situation and demand that the persons crossing the border undergo the appropriate procedure. But if, geographically speaking if the terrain is rugged, it's inaccessible, it is impossible to go into this 100-metre wide belt to effect any kind of control and if this area is important for security or defence reasons, then at the proposal of the defence department or the department of the interior this belt can be extended to include some other points where this kind of control can be effected, where illegal crossings can be prevented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You see Article 6, maybe you can help us out, because you see it makes reference to an international border crossing and then local border crossings, and it speaks of citizens of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in order for them to sojourn into certain zones of the neighbouring state. Can you please explain to us the difference between an international border crossing and a local border crossing, what is meant by this?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: International borders crossings are crossings used by persons and goods, and in the decision that we saw before, those are international border crossings. At the international border crossings goods can be cleared through the customs and cars, trucks, and so on can cross the border. Local border crossings cannot be used by trucks transporting goods because goods cannot be cleared through the customs, cannot be exported, cannot be imported. They can be used only by the residents of the municipality where those crossings are situated, enabling them to cross into the neighbouring municipality where they either work or they have fields where they have to do some farm work. So for instance people from Mostar cannot use those crossings. They cannot even cross them as persons even if they don't have any goods in their possession. They have to go to the international border crossings. But residents of Ljubuski, a municipality that borders Croatia, they can use the local border crossings and cross into Croatia, do whatever work they have to do. There is the police, there is a customs office at the local border crossings, but they're only there to check the identity of the persons crossing. These still the case today, and we refer to shows border crossings as local border crossings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 02187. 1D 02187. This is a report and it's from the Ljubuski Public Auditing Service, SDK. Perhaps you can explain this to us.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a typical report from the SDK where a branch office in the Ljubuski municipality submits a report about the collection of sales tax and other taxes, and as you can see from this document, the sales tax on the sales of goods emptied by the Mostar HVO, so we're talking about the 75 per cent of the sales tax collected in Ljubuski by the 1st of April it was taken out for the HZ HB budget, and the 25 per cent, the 39.000 -- or 39 million, that would be the 25 per cent that was taken out by the Ljubuski municipality. So this is just a report on the current situation indicating how it functioned between the municipalities and the HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Unless there are any questions on this document, I'll move on. 1D 01679. If we could look at this particular document. And again this is just as an example. Could you tell us first of all whether you're familiar with the document and whether you can identify what it is to start with.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with this document. I saw it in the course of the proofing. This is a document from the Elektroprivreda public company. It's actually the payroll for the employees where you can see the taxes, contributions and wartime tax that was levied on the salaries in accordance with the regulations valid in HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now this is May 1993. Or actually the -- this is the wages for May 1993. The document was generated, it would appear, 12 June 1993 and of course we see the levy on wages is 90 per cent and then we have another 10 percent is the war taxes, is that correct, on the first page?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 10 per cent, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go to the page 2, again this is for other purposes. We can see that the head of the directorate Zulfo Robovic, is he a Croat or is he a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now I'm going to go through the rest and I'll ask you, then I'll point to various numbers, and again it's for other purposes, but on page 3, for instance, number 5 and number 16, are they Croat or Muslim?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What page? What page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This would be 3 in English. It's -- and it may be easier if you just look at the English version.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Number 5 and number 16.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number 5, Ruso Begovic [phoen], well, they are Muslims, and Jugo, and number 16 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And 16 as well?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, 5 and 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And going to page 4, number 17, number 18, number 20, number 24, number 26, number 27. Can you please tell us whether they're Muslim or Croat?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Going to page 5, number 6, number 13, number 14, number 15. Croat or Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Page 6, number 1, number 3, number 4, number 9, number 10, number 12, number 13, number 15. Croat or Muslim?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Page 7. Number 16, number 18?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Page 8. Number 4 and number 7. Croat or Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 4 and 7.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslims. Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Page 9. These are wages for May 1993. This is number 3, number 11, number 12, number 14.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Page 10, number 3, number 4 number 8.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on to the next document, 1D 02136, and this is a conclusion, and it's dated 5 July 1993, and it says here under point 1: "The finance department is obliged in relation to defence financing to make the estimate of inflow of funds into the budget of HZ HB for the month of July 1993." Now, first I'm going to ask you to comment about this document, this conclusion, what is it; and number two and more importantly, I wanted to ask you about this word "obliged." Is this an instruction? Are you being instructed? Are you be ordered? What does the word "obliged" mean in the context with the way the HVO HZ HB operated under the statutory decisions and other regulations?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So after the conflict in Mostar broke out, the finance department was no longer functioning, and it was relocated to the municipality of Siroki Brijeg for a while, and in that period the SDK in Mostar no longer functioned, and the central unit was temporarily related to Siroki Brijeg, and again the municipalities exploited the situation and failed to implement, to enforce the Herceg-Bosna regulations. After the situation was analysed at the -- at a session of the HVO HZ HB, this conclusion reaffirmed our obligation to determine the monthly and quarterly budgetary revenues as indicated in the decree on the budget, because that decree stipulated that the departments had to plan their needs on a monthly and quarterly basis. So this conclusion reaffirms our obligation to do so, because it was necessary to get the system functioning again as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If you look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If -- thank you, Mr. Karnavas. Speaking from -- from a simple mind of a non-financial expert, is this to be understood in the sense that the government, Mr. Prlic and his colleagues, want to know how much money will be available in -- for July so that they can plan how much they can spend for defence purposes? Is that the idea behind it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. My department had to say how much we could expect in terms of real revenue in July, for the month of July, and this was actually the result of the situation that I was telling you about, because we were unable to do that in June and in May because of the situation as it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And just a point of precision. This is a conclusion. We could see that this is signed by Dr. Jadranko Prlic, but whose conclusion is this?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the conclusion reached at the session of the HVO HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So it's the collective body that's making this conclusion and not Dr. Jadranko Prlic, because we see his signature there?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go to the next document, 1D 01934. This is 12 August 1993. We see that -- that it is a document that you prepared as the head of the finance department. It's -- we see all this lovely legislation and instruments that are passed for the financial institutions to function. Now, if you could comment, please, on this report, especially if we look at, for instance, in the second paragraph towards the bottom half you seem to be indicating that all things are not operating as envisaged by the legal instruments that were drafted and adopted by the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the HVO HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a memo that I sent to the Croatian Defence Council and the presidents of the municipal HVOs about the functioning of the financial system. As I say here, after the regulations were passed and after efforts were made for them to be enforced, in the first six months of 1993 this appeared to be functioning with the application of all the mechanisms that we had put in place. After the conflicts broke out, particularly the conflicts in Mostar, and after there was a disruption in the functioning of the SDK and other institutions that had to be relocated to other places because of combat operations, the municipalities again exploited the situation to channel the revenue meant for the HZ HB budget to their own accounts. And in this context, on the 4th of August, I had a meeting with the heads of the municipal finance offices. And on the 5th, in Siroki Brijeg, there was a meeting with the presidents of the municipalities where we warned them that this kind of conduct was not acceptable and that they could cause great problems for the functioning of the HZ HB in terms of the defence and the functioning of civilian -- civilians' lives. At those meetings we concluded that in fact we had to comply with the existing regulations and reinforce the control and collection and that the municipal HVOs had to adopt their own budgets because they did not have their budgets, although there was no reason for that to be so. Of course here we again see this conflict. We talked to the presidents of the municipal HVOs, and at the same time they're members of the Presidency of the HZ HB, and they are the persons who are in fact responsible for the functioning of the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that's what I was going to be asking you, that essentially in Siroki Brijeg on 5th August when you're warning the representatives of the municipalities, which are the presidents as you've told us, essentially you have the Presidency there, albeit it's not a Presidency meeting. They're sitting there individually and collectively. Do I have it right?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And collectively, at least from yesterday as I understood you correctly, they're the legislative body that sits above the executive HVO HZ HB?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and they are there as the Presidency of the HZ HB and as such they had to in fact warn me that regulations had to be enforced and not the other way around. In reality I was there to warn them in their capacity as the presidents of the municipal HVOs that they had to enforce the regulations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, we need to have a break, a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go on to 1D 02135 and we're going to have to speed it up just a little bit. No, I'm sorry, I believe we covered this. No? Oh, we didn't. This is another conclusion where under 1 it says: "All bodies, offices, commissions, and services are obliged to present their needs for the period of October-December, so that the draft budget of the HR HB could be defined." Just very briefly again, I think I understand this but could you please comment on it?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the establishment Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, at one of the meetings in September the conclusion is adopted to update the implementation of the law on the budget of the HZ HB which says that revenues are planned on a quarterly basis, revenues and expenditures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now we're going to look at a series of documents to sort of put things into perspective.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're going to look at a series of documents that put things into perspective and shows how things were supposed to operate or did operate at least in part. And we'll start off with 1D 02132. That is a decision on the allocation of funds for the needs of the Department of Justice, and if you could please tell us exactly -- explain this document for us.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when this was adopted in December 1992 there was no budget of the HZ HB, but the monies were spent in accordance with the decisions of the HVO HZ HB. A -- the relevant department, in this case the justice department, would make a relevant submission. This was, I believe, that they needed money for the renewal of buildings, et cetera. And based on their submission, the finance department stated how much money there was in the budget, and then the HVO decided about the allocation of that money for the needs of individual departments and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm dreadfully sorry, Mr. Karnavas, because I am disrupting you and I'm going a step back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Because we had this interesting document, number 1943 just before the break where you told off to some extent, told municipalities what their duty was and asked them to comply, and I would like to know whether there was any effect to that, whether you were successful with that letter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That letter was sent to all municipalities; to the president of the HZ HB, Mr. Boban; the president of the HVO, that is, the president of the HVO HZ HB, to be precise, and after that things started improving. Of course the municipalities always requested a transitional period of a month or two to pay for some liabilities they had incurred, but as of September or October, the situation had -- was significantly better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No problem. And, Your Honours, just so you know, coming attractions, after this particular chapter which I'm about to finish, we're going to go back and look at some municipal decisions during this period when now they have the legislation, see how it's being actually implemented on the ground. So hopefully that may generate more questions, perhaps even provide an answer or two on occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If you look at 1D 02131. This is a decision on granting funds for the needs of the subdepartment of education. The previous document was in December, I believe. This is now January 17, 1993. Could you please comment on this.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is also a decision on the allocation of funds, this time for the needs of the education, culture, and sports department. In late 1992 and early 1993, the HZ HB started accumulating some funds which put us into the position to effect such payments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We go to 1D 02133. This is 17 January 1993. This is a decision on the allocation of funds to the HVO Kotar Varos. Maybe you could tell us what is this Kotar Varos, and what is this money or this allocation all about?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kotar Varos is a municipality in Bosnia. Today that area belongs to the Republika Srpska entity. Under the decision on the establishment of the HZ HB, taking into consideration that this area was populated by Croats and it was our duty to take care of all areas populated by Croats, since they were in an extremely difficult situation this aid was granted to that HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And we're talking about an area within a municipality or are we talking about an entire municipality? Which of the two, just to make sure I understand.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is an area within the municipality of Kotar Varos.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we look at the next document, 1D 02114. This is a decision on monetary assistance to be granted to the HVO municipality of Sarajevo in the amount of it looks like 5 million Croatian dinar. If you could please explain this.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is practically the same approach as in the case of Kotar Varos. This is an allocation to the HVO that was operating in Sarajevo. This is assistance to Croat -- the Croats in Sarajevo to procure food, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 1D 02306. We're now in April 1993, 9 April 1993. This is a decision on allocating funds for the needs of the subdepartment, it says subdivision but I believe it should be subdepartment, for education, culture and sports. Could you please look at that and give us a quick commentary on it.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This decision was taken at a time when there was no budget for the needs of the of institutions mentioned here. I must say these are some institutions that could not be funded because the budget of the republic was not functional. Normally the university would have gotten money from the higher education fund, which is in Sarajevo. The institute of education was a regional institution, but the regional sees had disappeared and these other cultural institutions were co-financed by the republic, but at this time they were left without money, and the people there had been without salaries for quite some time, and this is aid which was proposed by the subdepartment for education, culture, and sports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And if I understand you correctly, had this not been a war period, in other words, if we were normal times and things were functioning, many of these institutions would have been paid out of the republican budget?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'm curious about one minor thing. I can see the symphony orchestra and the national theatre that are going to receive 1 million Croatian dinars and 1.800.000 Croatian dinars respectively. Did they both operate or was it only to pay the wages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is about the maintenance of the institutions that had been in existence from former times. The building of the symphony orchestra was destroyed due to the shelling by the JNA. It was -- it burnt down. And the national theatre was also damaged. There were no conditions for performances or concerts to be held, but some people stayed and this was meant for their salaries. Later, a string quartet was formed from what remained of the symphony orchestra and other smaller ensembles, and the actors from the national theatre joined the HVO's war theatre, wartime theatre, after conflict broke out in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a former Finance Minister, you know that certain amounts are earmarked for operational or maintenance purposes or at times for investment purposes. Is any such distinction to be found here in these amounts or is everything put together, which is the amount that is going to be dedicated to rebuilding buildings, which is the amount earmarked for paying salaries, between the operational budget and the investment budget? Is there any difference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the budget was not operational. If there had been a budget it would have been clear what was to go for salaries, what for other expenditures, and what for special purposes such as reconstruction, et cetera. This is the first money granted to these institutions and upon the proposal of the subdepartment of education, culture and sports. So for -- this is -- the proposal contains individual items, but this is only a summary in this decision. The individual items are contained in the proposal submitted to the HVO HZ HB. As we did not have a budget with the relevant analyses, the decision only mentions this lump sum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I guess that in the symphony orchestra there were Croats and Muslims as well as Serbs. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and there were also Russians and Romanians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we look at the next document which is 1D 02165, 1D 02165. This is a decision, as we can see, approving to the social welfare centres of the municipal HVO, and we can see the various amounts, dated 29 July 1993. Perhaps you can explain this decision for us?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upon the proposal of the subdepartment of social welfare issues, this decision was adopted about a one-off aid to social welfare centres and the individual municipalities due to the new humanitarian situation. This is a -- practically a one-off aid to these institutions that were active in social welfare in the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we look at the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas. A simple question. Mr. Tomic, we see these papers. Can we assume -- can you say that these sums were then actually paid to the recipients that we have here, or is there a step in between where maybe the end is not quite like the starting point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All decisions taken by the HVO HZ HB about payment have been implemented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If we look at the next document, 1D 02134. This is about the allocation of funds to the HVO Sarajevo with its head office in Kiseljak, and we can see the amount. Could you please explain this document.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO office Sarajevo, which was relocated to Kiseljak due to the circumstances, applied for -- applied for aid because they were unable to organise activities that would generate revenue, and in that context this decision was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And finally by way of example if we look at 1D 02137, we see another conclusion. This is now August 9, 1994. And if we look at Roman numeral I, it's for the needs of the HVO of the Hrasnica, in the amount of a thousand Deutschmarks. Do you know what this is about?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An HVO was established in Hrasnica too. That is a place in the outskirts of Sarajevo, and this is a decision to grant aid to that HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. To that area where Croats are living outside of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes. [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now very quickly we'll go through those other four documents. We can conclude this chapter, and the first one is 1D 01896. This is now 10 December 1993, and here we have a financial plan for the judicial bodies for 1994. We see that it's signed by the Minister of Justice, the then Minister of Justice, Kresimir Zubak. And now if you could look -- if you could go through this very quickly with us it might be -- it might be of some assistance to some of the previous questions asked of you concerning budgetary matters.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the HR HB was established and its government, Mr. Martinovic became minister and all departments were required to make budget proposals for all of 1994. It was considered that the conditions allow the creation of a -- of an inclusive budget of Herceg-Bosna. So this is a -- this is in connection with the financial plan of the judiciary bodies and similar plans had been to be drafted by other ministries as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And Mr. Martinovic was the minister of finance under the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And at that time what position did you hold?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So you were still within the -- now you went from being the head of the department of finance under the -- from the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna to being the deputy minister within the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, before we leave this document there maybe some matters of interest. On page 15, under items -- that would be in the English, but it's item 67, 68, 69, 70. If I could draw your attention to -- to that segment of the document. We see that it makes reference under 67 to the District Prison in Mostar; 68, the District Prison in Busovaca; 69, the District Prison in Gabela; and number 70, the District Prison in Orasje. Could you please explain to us what -- what prisons are we referring to here, if you know, that is, and I assume you do because of your position.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, this refers to civilian prisons, that is prisons for criminals. They are prisons that used to be called District Prisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And at the very end of this document, right before we see Mr. Zubak's name, and he was at the time Minister of Justice. Would you confirm that, that he was the Minister of Justice for the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We see here he says: "Minimal assets are budgeted for the existing prisons, i.e., penal organs." By any chance do you know what he means by that?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably greater funds had been requested, but the ministry had to abide by a certain frame -- framework amount, so they had to be realistic with regard to the budget, and all ministries in their planning documents would always state that the funds requested are minimal anyway so as to avoid their demands being further reduced in the process of decision-making.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, sir. This is a budget proposal for 1994 stemming from the Ministry of Justice. I looked at this project. The -- this amounts in total to 3 million Deutschmark, and this is addressed to the Ministry of Finance. What happens after that? What kind of procedure is applied? Is it the minister of defence who then adopts these projects -- this project and determines which should be allocated where? What happens after that? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once the ministries submit their proposals, these proposals are further treated by the Ministry of Finance. Most often the ministry would establish that the costs are much greater than the revenue that can be provided by the Ministry of Finance. Then the Ministry of Finance returns the documents for corrections and adaptation to whatever is possible. It isn't up to the Ministry of Finance to decide what does not need to be funded or what -- what is to be reduced. That's up to the line ministries to decide. The salaries were easily assessable because the sums were fixed, and other -- the other costs were then set in relation to the total -- the sum total of the salaries. What we could not easily assess were other expenses such as the procurement of equipment, et cetera, but that was left to the line ministries to adapt these items. So the requested funds and the planned revenues for that year were -- were balanced in a way, and a proposal was formulated which was sent to the HVO. This proposal would then be forwarded to the chamber of representatives of the HR HB, and then -- only then can the budget become a legally binding document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In light of the events and the war, you did not have imbalanced budgets, did you? Let me repeat my question. In light of the war and the events at the time, weren't you tempted to have imbalances on the budget?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the reason why the budget for 1992 and 1993 was not adopted at all, because the demands of the users were far greater than the realistically possible revenues that could come into the budget. When the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was established, when Mr. Martinovic came in, a procedure was initiated to get the budget and to get the revenues into the budget, the revenues that did not go through the budget of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. So we're talking about the amounts that the Croatian emigre community from Bosnia and Herzegovina remitted back into the country. This was now channeled into the budget, and in order to balance the 1994 budget a loan was obtained from the Hrvatska Banka bank in Mostar, because Mr. Martinovic had this idea, and he was willing -- he wanted the budget to become operational on the 1st of January regardless of the price, because we had to pay interest on this loan. This was a commercial loan. It was not financed from the primary issue, which is an option for countries which do have a central bank. And in the planning of the budget we were able to remove this deficit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Croatian bank in Mostar gave you a loan for what amount?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that -- well, I can't really tell you. I think it was 5 million German marks. This item was planned in the 1994 budget.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was the interest rate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I couldn't tell you off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And just for point of clarification, Mr. Martinovic came into the picture not with the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna as is reflected on line 8 of page 74 but the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at the next document, and this may assist -- assist us with some of the previous questions, 1D 02740. This is 10 February 1994, and if you could please tell us what this is, what this document is.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document. It is a report to the chamber of representatives about the revenues. The intent was to report once a month to the chamber of representatives, which is where the heads of the municipal HVOs were now, about -- to inform them about the enforcement of laws from the sphere of finance. This is why there are two categories in this report. First of all is the classic report about the revenues that had come in through the accounts, and then in the second part the report deals with the territorial aspect, how the revenue was collected from each municipality. So the representatives, including the presidents of the municipalities, were able to see that their municipalities paid disproportionately less than the others although the economic situation in their municipalities was better or the same as in others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we -- if we just stick with this document just for a couple of minutes, and we can turn to page 8 on the English side, English version, and I believe this would be the second part of the document. It says "Public revenue realised in the period of 1 January to 5 February 1994." And we can see that some areas are -- they have an income. There's a customs revenue column, and then there are some other columns. And then if we go down, there are other areas that appear not to be making any sorts of contributions or there's no data for them. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the category "Municipalities" you can see all the areas where Croats lived in accordance with the decision to establish the HZ HB, and this document was made like this on purpose, to show the representatives that precious few municipalities actually took part in financing a large number of people and needs that existed in the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and there are areas, municipalities that never actually started functioning as municipalities or as locations that could contribute some revenue to the budget of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And I trust this may have answered your question, Judge Trechsel. It must have been of some assistance. 1D 02741. Very quickly, what is this? This is dated 7 March 1994. Again we see it's Jozo Martinovic as the Minister of Finance, and could you please explain what this document is?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the report for two months' period. It is sent to the same address, and you can see the progress report, an element -- well, this report -- this monthly report was not required in accordance with the law on budget. It was submitted, in fact, in order to exert pressure on the municipalities to enforce the laws. It is also important to note here that in this period the synthetic attacks and contribution rates ceased to exist and the pension fund was re-established as was the health insurance fund. So it is no longer a case where all the monies went into the same account in the budget but now they were allocated to specific purposes, health care, pension insurance, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that's how it existed prior to the break-up of the war.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And finally 1D 02742. Just very briefly. We can see it's a similar document, but what is this document about?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the same thing. It's for the first quarter of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, we see a lot of -- a lot of legal instruments being passed through in a very short period of time. Can you tell us whether you as finance -- the head of the finance department, whether you were assisted by any other members of the HVO HZ HB in, for lack of a better word, designing this system and drafting these -- these instruments?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from a small team, there were at the beginning 4 or 5 of us, and at the end I think there were 9 or 11 employees in the department itself, the finance department. For the most part I communicated -- I was in contact with Mr. Prlic, who had experience working in the republican government and various state organs, and he was really best acquainted with how budget functioned. He knew about public finances and I could share with him some of my doubts about some solution and then incorporate that into the proposals for various decisions. Other colleagues also contributed in their various spheres of expertise, whether the legal wording was correct, whether some other elements should or should not be included depending on the actual sphere. And once the legislation office was set up, it actually did most of the work in that sphere.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas, just before it leaves the page, just a correction I believe on page 77, line 15. It says that it's for the first quarter of 1993, and I think the document indicates we're talking about the first quarter of 1994. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, were you acquainted with Dr. Prlic prior to getting involved in the Special Purpose Council, for instance?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was the president of the youth organisation in Mostar, Mr. Prlic was the secretary of the socialist league, one of the seven institutions that were part of the political system, in the former political system, and we worked together on many projects in this area where we both worked at the time, and later on we worked together when he was the president of the Executive Board in the town, and then when he left for Sarajevo we again worked together to a smaller extent, but we mostly worked together with some major projects that Sarajevo co-financed, infrastructure, water supply. At any rate, projects that were co-financed by the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Do you recall by any chance in what field he did his Ph.D. dissertation in economics, what specific topic? If you recall.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was something about exchange rates. I can't really recall. He is younger than I am, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now let's look at concretely what's happening at the municipal level during this period, and by way of examples we'll start off with Livno. And so I'm going to now turn your attention to 1D 00362, and we're going to go sort of -- these are in chronological order by way of municipality, so we can just look at one perhaps as a vignette and then if necessary we'll look at a couple others. This is 1 October 1992. This is a decision on the temporary financing of the municipal HVO by the citizens receiving pensions. If you look at Article 2, if you could please comment on this.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Livno is one of the municipalities where there were many old-age pensioners who had earned their pensions working abroad, in Germany, Austria, and so on, and they received the salaries through the Privredna Banka Sarajevo bank, through their main branch in Livno, and now an order is issued that when those salaries are paid out a tax is levied, a 10 percent tax, for the purpose of financing the HVO of the Livno municipality, and in Article 2 the bank is ordered that whenever those monies come in every month the bank has to take 10 per cent of those amounts and pay it into the account of the Livno municipality and then to transfer the rest of the monies into the accounts of the citizens. First of all, it is not within the jurisdiction of the municipal HVO and it indeed cannot issue any such orders to the bank, and if any kind of war tax is to be imposed then it must be paid by the end users after they already receive the money.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the record, we can see it was sent to the HDZ and SDA party -- political parties. That's at the end of the document. 1D 00315. This is a rather interesting decision on the conditions for buying and selling foreign currency, and we see that this is by the Livno municipality, but then when we look at Article 2, it talks about Livno and Tomislavgrad municipal HVOs. And then we can see Article 5 as well. It talks about foreign currency or foreign exchange. Can you comment on this very briefly?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can go back to the previous decision for a moment. You can see that this was sent to the main branch of Privredna Banka Sarajevo in Livno, the Splitska Banka bank, a Croatian bank that had its branch in Livno, and to the Privredna Banka Zagreb, its branch office in Livno. And now the Livno municipality in this decision authorises the Privredna Banka Sarajevo to buy foreign exchange with Livno and Tomislavgrad municipalities as the end beneficiaries, and this is not within its purview at all, and this does not have any foundation in anything. So this is just an effort to make do in the chaotic situation that reigned, but this is in violation of the regulations that were being passed by the HZ HB, because at that time there was already an order in place stipulating that the branch offices of the banks domiciled in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in this case the Privredna Banka of Sarajevo, that a bank should be established with a seat in HZ HB which could then perform all the tasks that a bank usually deals with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 0 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 1D 00316. This is a decision on municipal administrative charges for the registration of motor vehicles and we can see this is October 1992.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time the decree and the tariff for turnover tax was already in place. It stipulated how turnover tax and stamp duty is to be paid, the latter when vehicles are being registered. But in Herzegovina cars are more than just a means of transport. There is a large number of cars, and they are potentially a great source of revenue for the budget. And in this context the municipality, by imposing this administrative decision on imposing municipal stamp duty, in effect introduced a new form of tax valid only in the Livno municipality, which is in contravention of the regulations that the HZ HB had already passed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will have to stop now because it is just about a quarter to 2.00. The registrar has told me that you have had six hours and 22 minutes, to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have, I think, some time to go on this, but I hope to finish within 45 minutes more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That was the reason for rising to my feet. It would be helpful, I think perhaps for everyone, certainly for the Prosecution, if there was some indication of where we are in terms of scheduling. I appreciate Mr. Karnavas has said approximately another 45 minutes. I wonder about the co-accused. It would just be helpful to know, Your Honour, if we might get some estimates at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good afternoon, Your Honours. As far as I know, the Defence would use all the time allotted to it for the cross-examination. Now, as to how we're going to allocate this time, we don't know. We suppose that Praljak, Petkovic, and Stojic Defence would certainly cross-examine, and we will inform you tomorrow if any other Defence teams have any intention of cross-examining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Nozica, how much time will you need?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said all the time that the Defence is allotted, and that would depend on the time taken by my learned friend Mr. Karnavas. As far as I know, it's supposed to be three hours or perhaps a bit more, because he took more. So this is the only thing, the only reason why I can't tell you how much we intend to use until he has completed his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as indicated by our learned friend Mrs. Nozica, we have an internal arrangement about the allocation of the time allotted to us, three hours, three hours 20 or 40 minutes, and then we will probably divide that time amongst us.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really don't have anything to add to what my colleagues have said, but I can just conclude that as things are now, the Prosecution would not get to cross-examine the witness tomorrow. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Coric Defence has not yet decided to cross-examine or not, but we will consult our colleagues and then we'll see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as things are we will not be cross-examining this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott, you will undoubtedly not start tomorrow. That seems pretty clear. I wish everyone a pleasant afternoon, and we shall meet again tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
